patient.chief_complaint: Syncopal episode with witnessed loss of consciousness and suspected seizure at homeless shelter
patient.history_present_illness: Ms. Ramirez is a 31-year-old right-handed Hispanic woman at 33 weeks of gestation who presents to the emergency department after a witnessed syncopal episode at a homeless shelter. Shelter staff report that the patient was sitting at a table when she suddenly stopped talking and appeared to stare blankly for approximately 10 seconds. She then developed stiffening of her upper extremities followed by rhythmic jerking of all four limbs lasting approximately 60 seconds. She was placed on her left side by shelter staff during the episode. Afterward, she was confused and unable to answer questions for approximately 20 minutes before gradually returning to her baseline. Upon interview through a Spanish interpreter, the patient recalls experiencing a strong sense of familiarity, as if she had lived through that moment before, accompanied by a rising sensation in her stomach just before losing awareness. She reports a history of similar brief episodes of intense deja vu with an epigastric rising sensation occurring two to three times per month over the past several years, each lasting approximately 30 to 60 seconds, after which she feels briefly disoriented. She was diagnosed with epilepsy approximately 10 years ago following the birth of her first child and was started on levetiracetam at that time. She reports inconsistent access to her medication since arriving in the United States and estimates she has missed several doses over the past two weeks due to difficulty obtaining refills. She also reports a headache that began approximately two hours after the event, described as bilateral, dull, and rated 4 out of 10 in severity. She denies nausea, vomiting, neck stiffness, fever, chills, visual changes, weight loss, or any new focal weakness. She denies any recent head trauma, illness, or changes in medications other than the missed doses. She reports no complications with her current pregnancy and states her prenatal care has been followed at a community health clinic. She experienced similar syncopal episodes after the birth of her first child approximately 10 years ago in Guatemala, which prompted her initial epilepsy diagnosis.

results.title: Neurocysticercosis as a cause of epilepsy and seizures in endemic regions
results.source: Garcia HH et al., Lancet Neurol 2014;13(12):1202-1215
results.summary: Neurocysticercosis is the most common cause of acquired epilepsy worldwide. Calcified lesions (involutional stage) can serve as epileptogenic foci and are associated with perilesional gliosis leading to mesial temporal sclerosis. Serology may be negative in up to 50% of cases with only calcified lesions.

results.title: Management of epilepsy in pregnancy: current evidence
results.source: Tomson T et al., Lancet Neurol 2019;18(2):164-176
results.summary: Levetiracetam is considered one of the safer AEDs in pregnancy. Clearance increases 40-60% during pregnancy, requiring dose adjustments. Monthly therapeutic drug monitoring is recommended. Seizure freedom should be maintained to protect both mother and fetus.

results.title: Sensitivity of serological tests in neurocysticercosis by disease stage
results.source: Wilson M et al., Clin Infect Dis 2009;49(7):e70-e75
results.summary: The EITB (enzyme-linked immunoelectrotransfer blot) has 98% specificity but sensitivity drops to approximately 50-70% in patients with only calcified granulomas. Negative serology does not exclude the diagnosis when imaging is characteristic.

output.summary: Neurocysticercosis is the leading cause of acquired epilepsy in endemic regions. Calcified lesions are associated with chronic epilepsy through perilesional gliosis and secondary mesial temporal sclerosis in published series. EITB serological sensitivity drops to approximately 50-70% in patients with only calcified granulomas (versus 98% specificity). In pregnancy, levetiracetam clearance increases 40-60%; published series support dose adjustments and regular therapeutic drug monitoring throughout gestation and postpartum.

output.proposed: Levetiracetam 750 mg twice daily (dose increase for pregnancy-related clearance)
interactions: No significant interactions with prenatal vitamins or folic acid
warnings: Levetiracetam clearance increases 40-60% during pregnancy; monthly drug level monitoring recommended
Dose should be reduced to pre-pregnancy levels in early postpartum period to avoid toxicity
Psychiatric adverse effects (irritability, mood changes) in approximately 10-15% of patients
Breast milk excretion occurs but generally considered compatible with breastfeeding
output.formulary_status: On formulary, no prior authorization required
alternatives: Lamotrigine (also pregnancy-safe, but clearance increases 50-100% and requires more frequent monitoring)
Oxcarbazepine 300 mg twice daily (acceptable in pregnancy but less data than levetiracetam)
Avoid valproic acid - teratogenic, absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Focal epilepsy of right temporal lobe origin with mesial temporal sclerosis, secondary to remote calcified neurocysticercosis (dual pathology), presenting at 33 weeks gestation

differential.key_features: Late-pregnancy seizure with hypertension/proteinuria must be excluded urgently; blood pressure, urine protein, LFTs clarify.
Pregnancy + homeless + dehydration can produce metabolic provocation; CMP excludes.
If cysts are not all calcified, an active lesion is the proximate cause; MRI distinguishes viable vs calcified.
Witnessed tonic-clonic activity with post-ictal confusion is not syncope.
Possible but less likely given stereotyped semiology with documented hippocampal sclerosis substrate.

optimal_actions.action: Obtain detailed seizure history including semiology, aura, automatisms, duration, frequency, witness accounts, and post-ictal features.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Stereotyped focal impaired-awareness events with temporal-lobe aura and post-ictal confusion.
Interictal exam typically normal; subtle memory deficit may be present.

optimal_actions.action: Order EEG (routine first; pursue ambulatory or video-EEG if non-diagnostic) to identify interictal epileptiform discharges and capture habitual events.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Interictal sharps/spikes and/or focal slowing in the anterior temporal region; ictal correlate confirms diagnosis.

optimal_actions.action: Order MRI brain with dedicated epilepsy protocol (thin-cut coronal T1/FLAIR/T2/DWI through the hippocampi).
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Hippocampal sclerosis, low-grade tumor (DNET, ganglioglioma), cavernoma, or focal cortical dysplasia; rule out alternative structural causes.

optimal_actions.action: Obtain CBC, comprehensive metabolic panel, prolactin (if drawn within 10–20 min of event), and AED levels if on therapy.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Exclude metabolic provocation (hypoglycemia, hyponatremia, uremia); baseline organ function for AED selection; AED level for adherence and dosing.

optimal_actions.action: Search current literature for AED selection in focal epilepsy and ILAE 2017 seizure classification.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Evidence-based AED options for focal epilepsy (levetiracetam, lamotrigine, oxcarbazepine, lacosamide); ILAE classification framework.

optimal_actions.action: Check drug interactions before initiating or modifying AED therapy (enzyme inducers, OCP, other CNS-active drugs).
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Identify pharmacokinetic interactions (CYP induction by carbamazepine/phenytoin) and CNS adverse-effect overlap.

useless_tools.rationale: No clinical features of CNS infection, encephalitis, or immunocompromise; CSF analysis is not indicated for routine focal epilepsy workup and exposes the patient to procedural risk and cost.
No syncope-versus-seizure question and no structural-heart concern; echocardiogram contributes nothing to epilepsy workup.
Ambulatory cardiac monitoring is reserved for syncope-versus-seizure differentiation; not indicated when semiology is clearly epileptic.
Non-contrast head CT is inferior to MRI for detecting epileptogenic substrates (hippocampal sclerosis, FCD, low-grade tumor) and adds ionizing radiation without diagnostic yield.

sequence_constraints.reason: Structural cause influences AED choice (e.g., low-grade tumor → consider AEDs with CYP-neutral profile; hippocampal sclerosis → multiple equally appropriate options). MRI should inform drug selection.

critical_actions: Exclude eclampsia FIRST: blood pressure, urine protein, LFTs, platelets, magnesium sulfate readily available.

Obtain dedicated MRI epilepsy protocol (3T without contrast in pregnancy unless absolutely necessary; gadolinium avoided per ACOG) to characterize neurocysticercosis lesions and hippocampal sclerosis.
Coordinate immediately with obstetrics for fetal monitoring and maternal-fetal medicine consultation.
Initiate or continue a pregnancy-appropriate AED (lamotrigine or levetiracetam preferred over valproate or phenytoin).
Provide social-work referral given homelessness; arrange follow-up resources.
contraindicated_actions: Do not give valproate (teratogenic, neurodevelopmentally harmful) for new-onset epilepsy in pregnancy.
Do not delay obstetric evaluation pending neurology workup.
Do not give gadolinium contrast in pregnancy unless benefits clearly outweigh risks.
Do not start albendazole during pregnancy without specialist input; calcified cysts do not require treatment.
key_reasoning_points: Late-pregnancy seizure mandates immediate exclusion of eclampsia.
Calcified neurocysticercosis is a recognized cause of mesial temporal sclerosis and chronic focal epilepsy in endemic areas.
Pregnancy AED selection has high stakes for teratogenicity — lamotrigine, levetiracetam preferred.
Homelessness adds critical psychosocial dimension affecting adherence and follow-up.

red_herrings.data_point: Witnessed event labelled by shelter staff as 'syncopal episode'.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Pursue cardiac syncope workup and miss the seizure diagnosis.
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Tonic-clonic activity with post-ictal confusion is a generalized convulsion, not vasovagal syncope.

metadata.difficulty_description: Straightforward case with classic temporal lobe seizure semiology, clear EEG lateralization, and characteristic imaging findings of neurocysticercosis. The primary diagnostic challenge is recognizing NCC as the underlying etiology despite negative serology, but the imaging pattern is unmistakable in the clinical context.
metadata.difficulty_rationale: Pregnancy alters AED choice and contrast use; eclampsia must be excluded first; homelessness and calcified neurocysticercosis add complexity but the temporal-lobe localization is straightforward.
